newsitem.title: UK: UK's Prescott takes Tube to unveil transport plan.
newsitem.headline: UK's Prescott takes Tube to unveil transport plan.

text.p: Deputy Prime Minister John Prescott marked World Environment Day on Thursday by announcing plans to cut car usage in Britain.
Prescott even eschewed his plush ministerial Jaguar car and took to London's underground rail system -- the Tube -- to hammer home his point.

"For too long, there has been an uncoordinated approach to the provision of transport and infrastructure services," said Prescott. "Transport decisions need to be integrated with the wider planning system and the way we and our children aspire to live and work in the future."
At a World Environment Day conference, he said it was his job to ensure polluters bear the costs and underlined his Labour Party's election pledge to use tax to tackle pollution.
"Tax is not a popular word. But environmental taxes can encourage industry to find cost-effective, innovative ways of reducing pollution," Prescott said.
He said the government would produce a "White Paper" policy document early next year to encourage people to use more public transport and leave their cars at home.
Britain has fewer cars per head than most European countries but uses them more due to poor public transport, he said.
City roads are consequently horribly congested and battles regularly ensue over plans for new highways that would cut through the nation's cherished countryside.
Ahead of the May 1 election it won in a landslide, Labour said Britain's roads were choked, its public transport neglected and crying out for investment.
It pledged to generate more infrastructure spending through partnerships between the public and private sector.

Britain's railways operator Railtrack Plc was criticised by the rail regulator Ofrail on Thursday for not investing enough in infrastructure despite posting profits of 339 million pounds ($553.2 million) in its first year since privatisation.
Prescott pledged to "toughen up" on investment, saying the transport system should be effective, efficient, clean and safe.

"It should provide genuine choice to meet the transport needs of all sectors of society. It should enhance local, regional and national competitiveness and development, and it should do so while respecting the environment and taking into account the costs transport itself imposes," he said.
